headline: Referred kratom sales ban back to committee; approved Office of Youth Services reorganization 11-2; nominated Shirley Tomlinson to Ward 6 School Committee.
summary: Public comment covered parking near the Hartnett lot, a proposed 16-story building, school board nominations, and property revaluations. Aldermen also discussed a state police investigation at the Office of Youth Services and a projected $508,000 general fund surplus. They confirmed Donald Spencer to the Ward 7 School Committee and approved a revised subordination agreement for 31 Central Street.
decisions: Approved the consent agenda, which included traffic rules, staffing changes, and committee reports.
Approved reorganizing the Office of Youth Services, including a memorandum of understanding with the Manchester School District, 11-2.
Referred the kratom sales ban ordinance to the Special Committee on Alcohol, Other Drugs & Youth Services, with Alderman Sapienza opposed.
Accepted, with regret, the resignation of Dan Bergeron from the Ward 6 School Committee.
Nominated Shirley Tomlinson to fill the Ward 6 School Committee vacancy, 9-4.
Confirmed appointments to the Police Commission, Planning Board, and Zoning Board as presented.
Confirmed Donald Spencer to the vacant Ward 7 School Committee seat, term to expire January 2028.
Approved a revised subordination agreement on the city's lien at 31 Central Street.
Accepted the FY 27 budget projections report, which showed a projected $508,000 general fund surplus.
Accepted donated funds for signage at the Theodore L. Gatsas Municipal Complex, with Alderman Kaw-uh opposed.
Referred $63,753.12 for ARPA roads and sidewalks and a part-time planner to the Committee on Finance.
Referred a $30,000 domestic violence prosecutor funding item to the Committee on Finance.
Approved Manchester Development Corporation permission to issue a $200,000 Custom MHT Loan to White Birch Living LLC.
Approved updating elderly, disabled, and blind exemption benefit amounts to align with the citywide revaluation.
Approved six community improvement funding resolutions, including $1,630,167.75 for Amoskeag EB & Canal Ramp work, to be enrolled.
Approved ordinance changes for the Human Resources Generalist and Administrative Compliance Coordinator positions, with Alderman Sapienza opposed.
Kept the $20,800,000 bond resolution for the 2027 Raise project on the table.
Kept the sewer ordinance on per- and polyfluorinated alkyl substances (PFAS) on the table.
Kept the petition to discontinue part of North Church Street on the table.

## BOARD OF MAYOR AND ALDERMEN

October 20, 2026 at 7:00 PM

Mayor Ruais called the meeting to order.

Mayor Ruais called for the Pledge of Allegiance; this function being led by Alderman Barry.

A moment of silence was observed.

The Clerk called the roll.

Present: Aldermen Kaw-uh, Goonan, Dexter, Fajardo, Bonilla, Kantor, Trisciani, O’Neil, Terrio, Sapienza, Burkush, Barry, Vincent

Absent: Alderman Thomas

Mayor Ruais: I have two acknowledgments that I'd like to make this evening. If we could please have Assistant Fire Chief Flurey come forward. I know this is tough, but we want to recognize you. City of Manchester, a Resolution: Whereas Assistant Fire Chief Flurey has dedicated more than 27 years of distinguished and faithful service to the Manchester Fire Department and the citizens of Manchester, demonstrating an unwavering commitment to public safety, leadership and community service. And whereas Assistant Chief Flurey began his career with the Manchester Fire Department on August 23rd, 1999, and through his dedication, professionalism and leadership, earned successive promotions to Lieutenant on March 7th, 2010, Captain on August 2nd, 2020, Battalion Chief on May 23rd, 2021, and Assistant Fire Chief on December 31st, 2023. And whereas, throughout his career, he has exemplified the finest traditions of the fire service, earning the respect and admiration of his fellow firefighters, colleagues and the community he has proudly served. And whereas, recognizing the importance of fostering relationships between the fire department and Manchester's youth, he organized the elementary school junior fire muster for more than 20 years, providing generations of Manchester school children with an opportunity to learn about fire safety and teamwork. And whereas, understanding that strength of a fire department extends beyond the emergency scene, he has organized the department's annual fishing trip, promoting camaraderie, friendship and lasting bonds amongst its members. And whereas, he has also demonstrated his deep appreciation for those who served before him by organizing the department's Retirees Christmas party, ensuring that retired members remain connected to the Manchester Fire Department family and that their years of service continue to be recognized and celebrated. And whereas, Assistant Chief Flurey's contributions reflect a career defined not only by professional accomplishments and advancement through the ranks, but also by his genuine commitment to the people, traditions and brotherhood of the Manchester Fire Department. Now, therefore, I, Mayor Jay Ruais of the City of Manchester, do hereby recognize and commend Assistant Chief Flurey for his exceptional dedication, outstanding leadership, and more than 27 years of honorable service to the City of Manchester.

Mayor Ruais: Brenda Masewic Adams, please come forward. City of Manchester, a Resolution: Whereas Brenda has been honored with the New Hampshire Department of Motor Vehicles Municipal Agent Excellence Award in recognition of her exceptional leadership, innovation and dedication to public service as the City of Manchester's municipal agent. And whereas she has transformed the office of the tax collector through strategic improvements, technological innovation, and a commitment to collaboration, open communication and accountability, expanding services and creating more accessible and efficient ways for residents to conduct business with the city. And whereas her leadership has resulted in significant improvements to municipal operations, including online payment services, enhanced customer service systems, and initiatives that have saved the city more than $350,000 over the last 14 years, demonstrating her commitment to responsible stewardship of public resources. And whereas, Brenda and her team managed the largest motor vehicle registration customer base in New Hampshire, processing more than 160,000 transactions annually while continuing to prioritize the needs of residents and businesses. And whereas her contributions extend beyond motor vehicle registrations to include property tax collection, where her leadership has strengthened the city's financial stewardship, recovering delinquent taxes and sewer charges, and supported affordable housing efforts through the sale of city owned properties. And whereas Brenda exemplifies the highest standards of municipal leadership through her dedication to mentoring employees, encouraging accountability, fostering collaboration, and empowering her team to continually seek better ways to serve the community. Now therefore, I, Jay Ruais, Mayor of the City of Manchester, do hereby recognize and congratulate Brenda on receiving the New Hampshire Department of Motor Vehicles Municipal Agent Excellence Award, honoring her outstanding accomplishments, innovative leaderships, and enduring commitment to the residents and businesses of Manchester. It's important to note that Brenda was the first ever recipient of this award.

PUBLIC COMMENT

1. Mayor Ruais advised that the purpose of the public comment session is to give residents of Manchester the opportunity to address the Board. All people wishing to speak must sign up with their name, address and topic. Once called, they will have up to three minutes to speak and any comments must be directed to the chair and concluded when their time is up. If the Clerk calls their name and they are not present to speak, they will not be given a second opportunity. Any

resident wishing to speak will come forward to the nearest microphone, clearly state their name and address when recognized and give their comments.

Mother Paul, 279 Cartier Street: This is regarding the parking lot over on Lowell Street. I don't know if any of you have really thought about how much traffic comes out of the cathedral after masses, and especially when we have very big events. There's over a thousand people in the church. And so when you think of the people coming out of the church and buses, when we have kids that are coming from all the schools and coming to the cathedral for some event, what will we do and where will the people park? It becomes a very big issue. So we're really asking you to consider, because there are really three churches that use that parking lot on not just Sundays, but on other days when they have events going on in the church. It's a big concern. And one of the other things I was questioning when I was here the last time and they had the schematic up on the board, you could see the building, but you couldn't tell what side of the building the restaurants were. And it looked like from where I was sitting in the back that the restaurants opened up onto Lowell Street. And if that is accurate, that's even more traffic, more cars. And, you know, I've heard business people in the city talking about how difficult this is going to be for those that own businesses, especially restaurants who don't really have any parking on the side streets in Manchester and saying, what are we going to do for parking? I just want to bring the parking issue up again. I know it's really big and thinking of people who are disabled that come to church having to go into a parking garage and I think it is going to be a very difficult thing and something we have to think about. What do we do in situations like that? I just want to bring that forward for you to consider. And I appreciate your listening. God bless you all.

Meghan Moore, 220 South Mammoth Road: I also am questioning the parking lot issue at 99 Lowell Street for the same reason: the churches, the library, and things around there. I have friends who have parking permits. What are they going to do for their parking? And not only is it important that we address this parking, I know we want to have more business, but when people go to the church and to the library and to these things on Sundays or whatever, they go to other places and they park in this parking lot. And I drive by this parking lot on various times of the day, weekends, whatever; on weekends, it's always full. On the weekdays, it's half full, it's a quarter full. I know that this project, I know we want to build up Manchester and we want to do all that. I think that's great, but I think we have other places to put this building. And when these people were here, they were like, well, this isn't about the parking lot. We already have the building. We already can put it there. And we're saying, well, we didn't know about the parking. If you put the building there, where are we going to park? And this is a big issue, and I love the fact that we want to have more buildings. I totally love that. I get it, put them wherever, but we need the parking there. There's no other places to park, and if we want people to come to downtown Manchester, they have to park.

Jose Marte, 62 Trahan Street: A lot of you know that I'm running for state office, and a lot of you guys know that about three or so years ago, I ran for alderman and I lost. Upon my losing, I had a conversation with Jim. Jim had told me that the changes that I want were not on a local level, so I ran for state. Let me explain to you guys that things have gotten so much worse every single goddamn year. Two years ago, I got a text message on Facebook, just got custody of my little girl, my second one, my oldest one. I have sole custody of my two girls that are now living with me. And for a guy to message me and for me to tell the police and for them not to do anything, it's outrageous. I got told that if I showed up at the polls, that my life would cease to end and my girls’ lives, too. And every single year it gets worse. Just last year, a pedophile by the name of Lee wanted my daughters at his house. When I told that to the police, there was nothing that they could do. This year I've had several death threats and I've had people messaging me disgusting messages, and I'll say them today. It is appalling how I get called a nigger and a spic on a weekly basis, just because somebody doesn't like that I'm a Republican. I've tried to have conversations with Democrats and it's 50/50. Not every Republican, not every Democrat, is a bad person. But I've seen a lot of hate coming from the Democratic Party, and it's outrageous. I have called your office, Jay, just to have a sit down and see what we could do. But the violence keeps going on. I've just had not so long ago, one of my political signs slashed to hell. And that's part of the reason why I'm here, because I called, and it seems like it's moving at a slower pace than I'd like it to. And there has been other things that have disturbed me, which is the false allegations that are going around. One lady wanted to throw me in jail so badly. Her idol was Jane Doe, falsely accusing people as fast as she could type on Facebook. I'm putting people down slowly with evidence. Jim's behavior Saturday was extremely disgusting, yelling at me and just saying what he wanted to, falsely accusing me. It was appalling. And your behavior should change. I never said anything bad against you until Saturday, and I am calling you a fraud for the person that you really are. You’re a fraud and people should know who you are.

Rich Girard, 283 Orange Street: Your Honor, you've gone overboard to justify not vetoing a school board nomination. You said the charter gives sole authority to the board to fill those vacancies, that the mayor has no role to play, and that the veto would be unprecedented. What you didn't say was that the board has never sacked a ward alderman's nominee. This leads me to ask which precedent is worse: vetoing clearly partisan nominees not supported by the ward alderman, or your feckless failure to defend against a clear attack on board protocol and ward representation by a partisan mob. The charter says, “the mayor shall have veto power upon the action of the Board of Aldermen in all matters. No vote can be passed or appointment made by the board unless a vote to override the veto is approved.” Clearly, you have a role to play. Alderman Kantor nominated Chastice Cocchiarella, whose resume shows her to be the kind of working class woman Democrats claim to care about, with jobs ranging from loan officer to waitress to office administrator to sales manager to hotel desk clerk. She's a lifelong Manchester resident who has two girls in our schools, was a long time officer in the Weston PTO and is a taxpayer. She ran for the seat last year, losing to a formidable incumbent who himself was nominated to fill a vacancy by a ward six alderman. Countenance that against the nominee from Alderman Jason Bonilla, and stop to consider that, folks: an alderman from a different ward has nominated someone to represent people he does not represent. Is that a precedent that you want? The extolled virtues of this nominee include having a lifelong connection to Manchester, firsthand experience with our public schools, and someone who will soon have a daughter in school, giving her a, quote, personal and continuing stake in the success of our schools and the experiences of the families they serve. Sounds an awful lot like Chastice or ward seven nominee Randy Tremblay, who Christopher Potter lied about in his comments to this board. She knows Manchester because she grew up here, writes Bonilla, and knows our schools because she attended them. If those things matter, why did the Democrats support Donald Spencer, a transplant from Indiana who only came here to work for the state Democrat Party, which he did from 2018 to 2021? From 2021 to 2024, he was Cinde Warmington's executive council campaign manager, the caucus director for the Democratic Party Executive Council Campaign Committee, and deputy manager of Warmington's gubernatorial campaign. Mysteriously, none of this was on the resume sent by nominating Alderman Trisciani, who emphasized his extremely short tenure as a teacher, including as a substitute in two affluent, liberal, virtually all white suburban towns to support his nomination. Not to worry, though, his social media accounts fly rainbow flags, announce his pronouns, and support Black Lives Matter. His X account is private, though, so the public can't see his posts. Bonilla's nominee Shirley Tomlinson shares Spencer's advocacy for woke ideologies that have brought us trainings like Whiteness is Power and the Wheel of Power and Privilege. She's a board member of Black Lives Matter and is associated with other left wing activist groups that tout things like environmental justice. She works for the state in an operation formerly known as the Office of Health Equity. DHHS changed the name to avoid the obvious DEI focus, but her listed experiences demonstrate that her work is about identifying and labeling groups of people to further the privileged versus historically underserved, and oppressor versus oppressed narratives running rampant in our schools. Mr. Mayor, you can either restore order to the process and respect for the ward alderman and the neighborhoods that elected them, or run away from the mob. Whether or not you veto these nominations, which clearly you can do, show your voters your actual priorities.

Daniel Mowery, 112 Holt Avenue: Last evening, Mr. Mayor, I had a town hall meeting. I invited you, I invited Mr. O'Neil, I invited Ms. Trisciani. Neither one of you showed up, but our devoted alderman, Crissy Kantor, and our devoted State Senator, Victoria Sullivan, did. They heard the people. The people want Crissy Kantor’s nomination to go through. Ward five has no reason to be nominating a school board member. Ms. Trisciani was not there, so therefore she feels she should not be representing our ward. Mr. O'Neil has never been to one of our town halls, so that means that only Ms. Kantor should be the only one nominating anyone and everyone should vote for Chastice. Another thing, this parking in front of Saint Joseph's Church, I agree with Mother Paul. You know, that is a big parking lot. A lot of people go to Saint Joseph's and to the other churches around. You want them to walk three or four blocks to go to church? We're having a hard enough time getting people to come to church. Now, this just gives them another excuse to go outside of the city or to another church. Saint Joseph has been here for years and years. That is a gorgeous church. And you're going to put a 16 story building in front of that church and put a big eyesore. Saint Mary’ s is a big historic building in our city, and when you go into the city and you're on this side and you look on the west side, you see Saint Mary’ s. Are we going to see Saint Joseph's anymore because you're putting a 16 story building in front of it? It's ridiculous. Also on last Thursday, the New Hampshire Prostate Cancer Coalition, we had a fundraiser to raise money for the New Hampshire Prostate Cancer Coalition. I invited my social committee from Saint Pius Parish. A lot of them came down, but a lot of them refused because they don't feel safe walking from the parking lot or the parking garage. These are elderly people that go to the Palace Theater and if they don't feel safe, next the Palace Theatre will be closing. So you need to really think about not building that building.

Chastice Cocchiarella, 1484 Candia Road: I appreciate everybody coming out and giving their input to the city. First, I want to thank Crissy Kantor for nominating me for the ward six School Committee vacancy and believing in my ability to serve. I also want to thank the aldermen that took the time to speak to me, hear my perspective, and give me the opportunity to share why this matters so much to me. I understand everyone has a busy schedule, and I appreciate the time and consideration of the entire board, including those I wasn't able to connect with. My name is Chastice Cocchiarella. I'm asking for the opportunity to serve the community I call home. Manchester isn't just a city where I live, it's where I raise my daughters, where I invest my time, and where I want to see our children and families succeed. My passion for this truly began during my five years as treasurer and event chair for the Weston Elementary School PTO. In that role, I saw firsthand the struggles our students, teachers, staff and parents are facing. I saw how much our schools rely on dedicated people working together, often while trying to do more with limited resources. I wanted to do more than support our schools and our community through fundraising and events. I want to be part of the work that happens addressing these challenges, support our educators and give our children the best possible opportunity to succeed in all capacities. That experience also strengthened my understanding of responsible leadership, being accountable for decisions, earning people's trust, managing, carefully listening to different perspectives, and following through on commitments. It showed me how important it is to put students first and work together to make meaningful differences. In 2025, I ran for the ward six School Board Committee because I wanted to make a difference. I received 687 votes; 41%. I recognize that I did not win that election and I respect the outcome, but I also believe the level of the community’s support is meaningful. I didn't walk away after the election. My commitment to Manchester and its schools has remained. I know that serving on the School Committee comes with a great deal to learn. I am ready to do that work. I will come prepared, ask questions, listen carefully and learn from those with experience. My values are simple: honesty, integrity, accountability and treating people with respect even when we disagree. I believe public service is about doing what is right, being transparent, taking responsibility for your decisions, remembering who you represent. I would not take this appointment lightly, and I would work hard to earn your trust placed in me. Thank you for your time today. I'm asking for your vote and the opportunity to serve ward six.

Sophia Cocchiarella: I attend McLaughlin Middle School. I also attend the Boys and Girls Club of Manchester. I anticipate to be a CIT this summer at their summer camp in Bedford. I am also a part of the McLaughlin Middle School Band. I have done many events in the community, such as the Memorial Day Parade for three years now. I would also like to talk about the new construction at my school. I would like the old bathrooms to be redone as well, because they're still old and not all of the toilets still work, and the water bubblers as well. They're not always very good and working correctly. The filters are not changed very often, as they should be. I think the new construction of the school is really nice because I get to class much faster. I don't have to walk across the building. I think my mother would be very good in the School Board because she has had much experience in the school because I've been in school for 13 years. Well, I've been a citizen of Manchester for 13 years. I was born at Elliot Hospital and I've been going to school for about nine years now and I'm in the eighth grade. I'm very excited to be attending Memorial High School next year and being a part of band and having fun with my friends and all that.

Avery Cyr, Ward 3: I was really frustrated to hear that when a School Board member passes away in office, like with Bob Baines, or resigns, School Board members are appointed by the Board of Aldermen. I think that's really not fair to the people, because the people have the right to make their voices heard, and the Board of Aldermen should work to have special elections, instead of cutting out the people's voice and appointing them, because the people might not want the person who the board is appointing because their opinions change every day. It's completely unfair and undemocratic to the people. And if I'm ever elected to the Board of Aldermen myself, I will be vehemently against appointing members. If it was within six months of an election, then sure. But a year before the next election is absolutely not acceptable, and I think the board should end that practice when a seat becomes vacant on the School Board. I don't have any problem with the people who may be appointed. I just don't think that we should be appointing people in general.

Brittany Ping, 199 Putnam Street: I'm here because I agree with the gentleman before me. What we participated in two weeks ago was voter disenfranchisement. One of the things that the electorate, when they elected you, to do as alderman, was to participate in the presentation of candidates for your ward in the instance of a School Board vacancy. This is a long standing tradition in the city of Manchester. I'm going to call it voter disenfranchisement. That happened two weeks ago, because we did have a qualified candidate. So what happened from my perspective, as a member of the public, is the School Board member from ward seven presented a candidate. And when he came and did his three minutes, the previous school board member from ward seven said that a Democrat should hold this seat, and a Republican should not hold the seat. And someone who supported school choice should not hold this seat. So while I definitely agree with what this gentleman said, that if we truly believed in a democratic process, if we believed in our constitutional republic, the thing he recommended would be a charter amendment that this board could present, and we could hold a public notice. But if not, I will help any of you present a charter amendment that says only a Democrat could hold a Board of School committee seat, or only somebody who only believes that the Manchester school district, and this SAU, is the appropriate education for a child in the city of Manchester, should hold that seat. And we all know every single one of you, in the kindest way, know that that is unconstitutional. It's unconstitutional to make that charter amendment. It would not stand up in court. And so I'm not saying that we as the public don't have a right to come to our alderman, but they did go to their alderman. The public did go to their alderman, and I understand that the charter is unclear, but the history of the city of Manchester is not unclear. And the way that this Board of School Committee candidate was presented in ward seven is voter infringement, and it's unconstitutional boundaries where this School Board Committee said that seat should never be held by a Republican or anyone who supports school choice. We just said that our charter schools don't matter in this city. We just said our home schoolers do not matter in this city and do not deserve a voice in the city of Manchester. And we said that our children who utilize things like the Children's Scholarship Fund to escape bad situations or education freedom accounts to be educated in our city, which is the minority of students in the city of Manchester. They don't deserve to have a fraction of a representation in our city governance because guess what? You as the alderman, you are the checks and balances of that system. And so if you believe that, if you believe in that voter disenfranchisement, I ask you to please ignore Crissy Kantor's excellent recommendation.

Victoria Sullivan, South Beech Street: I'm also a Senator representing District 18. I have people reaching out to me daily who are in fear of losing their homes because of the costly decisions this board made. At a recent meeting, Alderman Trisciani made a statement that that was fear mongering when I said that. It is now reality. People are calling me daily because they say they cannot stay in the city because of the decisions that this board has made. I've shown up here for the better part of 20 years, fighting for the children and families of this city. I've called out Republicans and Democrats alike when you are making decisions that would ultimately hurt our city. But I've never been angrier than I am today. The overwhelming majority of this board campaigned on lower taxes and respecting the tax cap. And you lied. You lied to your voters. You lied to get in these seats and you betrayed people. And some of you are smirking at me because you think this is a game where you think this is funny; you're not talking to your constituents and you don't know what they're going through right now. I can tell you that by looking at your faces. I'm out there knocking on doors and literally had someone crying on my shoulder the other day because of the decisions that this board has made. Someone reached out to me because they have a house that's been in their family for over 100 years. They don't use it as a commercial space, but it has been deemed commercial property. It went from $700,000 to $1.2 million, and they have to leave the city. These are the decisions that you're making and these are impacting the children of this city. A child who has an empty belly or doesn't know where they're going to sleep, does not care about a $7 million skateboard park. They don't care that you're ripping up Hanover Street, which is in perfectly good condition and one of the best streets we actually have, to make it a vanity project for you all and get rid of parking so we can make this a carless city. It's insanity. What is happening in this city is absolute insanity. Alderman Fajardo: I don't want to put you on the spot. I am just seeking to understand who is dictating that? Is that your office arranging for the space for those hearings to take place? Is that Vision? Because it was very unclear to me as to who I should even ask my questions to. So obviously, I'm going to ask you because you're in charge at the end of the day.

C. Kurfehs: When we went down the road of trying to find a suitable area to house hearings, we ultimately chose the chambers just as being the largest public space. And the chambers and then the conference room off of the chambers. We couldn't foresee any type of a situation where the Vision staff might be put into or get themselves into a position where there's a problem that taxpayers have with not being able to discuss the process on a one on one basis. So it was once we learned that there was an issue in the case that you're referring to, we had a discussion with Vision and they essentially said it was a little bit of an unusual situation that had occurred at that time and that 95% of taxpayers are absolutely terrific and reasonable. And not to say that those taxpayers weren't terrific and reasonable, but it's possible that someone got a little louder than normal. And everybody's passionate about taxes. So that's something that is totally understandable.

Alderman Fajardo: All things being equal on who is at fault, what is in place going forward for the balance of the in-person hearings, whether they're hosted by your office or by Vision, for individual taxpayers to have their hearing in private?

C. Kurfehs: All of the hearings in the Assessor's Office will be one on one in one room.

Alderman Fajardo: What about the ones that Vision is going to hold?

C. Kurfehs: Vision at this point is doing very few hearings.

Alderman Fajardo: In person hearings?

C. Kurfehs: Yes.

Alderman Fajardo: Any hearings at all?

C. Kurfehs: In total they're ramping down. We had anticipated about 8% of all parcels that were going to hold a hearing based on what Concord went through in their revaluation recently. And we're only at about 3.5%. And so we just haven't had the volume that we had forecast. The Vision staff is cognizant of these issues that arise and they've assured me that they're doing all that they can to prevent a similar situation.

Alderman Fajardo: Excellent. And they, I assume, have your number.

C. Kurfehs: They have my cell phone number.

Alderman Vincent: I'm just going to throw out stuff, and I apologize in advance if I cut you off as you're talking. I just want to clarify this for everybody. Everything that Alderman Fajardo said was on point and certainly a concern. I just want to make sure that the process as a whole is as clear as it can be. I know there's a lot of people out there that are very upset. They're nervous, they don't understand the process. They think if they can't get in there by this first process, that they're done. They got to eat whatever it is. That is incorrect. That is not the case. This is phase one of the process. Phase two or the actual final phase would be the abatement process, which is done by application and you are accepting those applications, correct me if I'm wrong, until March 1st of 2027. C. Kurfehs: March 1st is the deadline. We will start accepting those applications anytime once tax bills start arriving.

Alderman Vincent: So this process is basically to help identify flaws or any value in corrections. So it's an early opportunity for somebody to have a correction before the bill comes out.

Charles Kurfehs, Assessor: Exactly.

Alderman Vincent: Which is a good thing. So after that it just needs to be known out there that this is not your final opportunity to have this fixed. If you truly feel, because a lot of people, two weeks is not enough time to get what they want, get their paperwork, they got work schedules, life, everything brings complications to that. So what needs to be heard to the people out there that own homes, property, anything like that, this is not the end all. You have an abatement process. You file an application, you gather your documentation, and then you're going to do another one. Now, obviously, most of these will start in sometime December or whenever they're going to start. So it's going to be after the bill. So everybody's going to have to pay their bill. But corrections will issue rebate at moment of decision, correct?

C. Kurfehs: We'll start reviewing those abatement applications immediately once they're received and not wait until after March 1st. And on a rolling basis, try to process them as fast as we can.

Alderman Vincent: Perfect. I've spoken with you earlier this week about some issues. In some ways, we can help this to be clear for the public out there. I'll ask you, and I know you're working on it, but the plan is to create some kind of document, something where the people can read it and it brings it to such a simplistic read where they understand the problems and they understand the process, and they can move forward with numbers, emails, whatever we can give them. Because there's just a lot of bad info out there, people are just putting a lot of garbage out there and it doesn't need to be out there. There is good information out there, but there's a lot of garbage too. I don't want the residents, the elderly, new homeowner that's never gone through this before, to fear this process. It's a cycle, folks. We do this. It's not the Board of Aldermen that made these numbers up. It's a process that we went by. So that being said, I just want to make sure that we work for the people. We try to make it as clear as we can, whether it be a document on your website or something that you push out to the aldermen, and we'll push it out to our constituents. And as always, I thank you for your efforts in this. I know it's not easy. You're doing a hell of a job, and I appreciate everything you do and what you'll continue to do.

Alderman Trisciani: If someone receives their bill in December and are having trouble paying it, my assumption is, and what I've been telling people, is they reach out to you immediately, and there's things we can put in place that we can help people.

C. Kurfehs: Yes.

Alderman Kantor: How did you go about advertising the extra days?

C. Kurfehs: We just learned of those extra dates yesterday afternoon from Vision actually it was right around 5:00. I'm going to be issuing more of an official statement that it will be posted on our website where people will be able to have an accounting, as Alderman Vincent had mentioned, of the various steps that need to be taken by taxpayers to be able to navigate the rest of the hearings and then also the formal abatement process.

Mayor Ruais: You'll send that to the Board so that we can respectfully share that with people that reach out and share to our social media channels as well. And we can send that to the press so we can notify the the public at large.

C. Kurfehs: Yes.

C. Kurfehs: Yes.

Alderman Bonilla: So if that's possible, can we get that as soon as possible?

C. Kurfehs: Yes.

Alderman Kaw-uh: During public comment, we heard some concerns about the proposed redevelopment of the Hartnett lot. I just wanted to give kind of a PSA for the folks who are listening in and for the board in general, the Planning Board kept that application open. And so it is coming back for a continuation of its public hearing the first Thursday of November. So Thursday, November 5th. So the Planning Board meeting will be at 6 p.m. here in the Aldermanic Chambers, third floor of City Hall. So if anybody wishes to watch or attend or to come speak, they are welcome to do so on that application. I also wanted to note, just for general understanding, that the proposal as it stands today currently does include more than 300 parking spaces. And it also has commercial spaces which open up to the south and to the west, not to the north or the east towards the churches. And obviously the board is still deliberating the matter, still talking. It will be talking to the applicant at that continuation. And the public is welcome to continue chiming in and providing their feedback.

Alderman Kantor: I was at the meeting and there is no public parking, correct?

Alderman Kaw-uh: At this time the parking is intended for, at least per the developers’ statement, for the residents and their visitors, so there would be no spillover parking onto the streets from the folks who would be living there or visiting the commercial businesses.

Alderman Kantor: So we don't know where the people attending the churches or the surrounding businesses are going to park.

Alderman Kaw-uh: There are a number of on street spaces in the general vicinity, as well as the Victory Garage, which is kitty corner to the Hartnett lot parcel. And again, if we are thinking of folks who have potential mobility issues and need help getting around, the board is happy to listen to all public comment on that and try to come up with potential solutions. Because we are definitely sensitive to that issue.

Alderman Kantor: How many public permits do we have for the people in the other surrounding areas that are residential, permitted parking?

Alderman Kaw-uh: I don't know the number off the top of my head, but I'll take a note. I do know that the fee is lower for the Hartnett lot than it is for the garage itself. And while the board has not made any, I think it's premature because the board hasn't made any official decision one way or the other, but if the board were to happen to approve this project in any capacity, I think it would be a good idea for this board to consider potentially asking the parking division to honor those parking permits at Victory Garage at the same price. It's a bit premature at this time for that, but I think that's important to keep in mind for sure.

Alderman Kantor: I do suggest, we've gone on field trips before, and I think it would be nice to go on a field trip to actually walk the area so we can actually see how hard it would be for someone who has a knee replacement, hip problems, anyone that has a problem and see how far it is. And actually, I think we should go in the dead of winter when it's really icy out. And I love DPW, I always brag about them, but let's be realistic, our sidewalks are never cleared good enough and it is very dangerous for people. So to have them walk all the way from the Pearl Street Garage all the way to the cathedral is to me, unacceptable.

Alderman Kaw-uh: The Planning Board itself has discussed that matter as well, especially given that winters here can result in a lot of snow. The applicant agreed already in some back and forth with the Planning Board that they would be responsible for the maintenance of those sidewalks in the winter, that they would be removing snow, keeping them free of ice. And that would take the load off of DPW as well. If this were approved, they would have maintenance folks per their representation, who would be doing that. They also have proposed completely rebuilding the corners of those intersections so that it's brand new, so there wouldn't be existing cracks or anything like that, as well as adding bump outs to reduce the crossing distance that pedestrians would need to take as they're trying to go from one side of the street to the other. One last thing that would require this board's deliberation on if it got to this point, this board could always consider creating more accessible parking spaces on the northern and eastern part of the lot where there's proposed future street parking. I don't know how many of those would be accessible by default, but this board could certainly, as far as I'm aware, require that more are made accessible. I think that would be a very reasonable thing to do.

Alderman Kantor: Question on what they said, they would take care of the snow removal. Is that from point A to the whole area, including from each garage, from Victory, from Pearl Street, will they be taking care of all of those?

Alderman Kaw-uh: Just on the block. So the square, essentially, that Hartnett lot would make.

Alderman Kantor: It's a long way to go for someone who is older or disabled to walk to church. I hope we're not trying to keep people from going to church, because that would be absolutely evil.

Alderman Dexter: There's been a lot of talk about my ward and this block, it's my understanding that this project, this lot was deemed surplus by this board. It was under a purchase and sale. It is out of this board's control necessarily as to what happens at that specific project. At this point, it's up to planning and zoning because we've given our ability to control those parts to planning and zoning. And if I'm not mistaken with that said, we can all go to planning, we all can go to zoning, we all can go to those boards and have our voices heard. Parking is definitely a concern in that area. And there is talks with the developer about outside of their project, them doing some other parking things in that area along the parks and seeing what we can come up with for extra parking. It sounds like based on some of the conversation we've had tonight, we as a board need to do a better job of budgeting for our DPW and giving them the money they need to do snow removal and making our sidewalks safer and accessible to our residents. We as a city should look at how we do things. Do we change the way that we go to church? Do we all park right out in front of church, or do we do a drop off and have one person drive? I don't know what the answer is, but those are all conversations that I am willing to have as the ward alderman for this project. And I welcome those comments and those emails and those phone calls. So if you need to know how to get a hold of me, my information is on the website and I'd love to hear from everyone. But those are some of the things that are going on with the Hartnett lot from the ward three perspective.
